newsitem.title: JAPAN: Ex-Japan cult member blames guru in kidnap - murder.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Japan cult member blames guru in kidnap - murder.

text.p: A former member of a Japanese doomsday cult told a court on Friday he was ordered to kill a lawyer's family by the cult guru accused of masterminding the 1995 Tokyo subway gas attack.

Asked by state prosecutors who had ordered him to kill Yokohama lawyer Tsutsumi Sakamoto, his wife and baby son, former Aum Shinri Kyo (Supreme Truth Sect) member Satoru Hashimoto blamed cult leader Shoko Asahara.
"All responsibility for the incident rests with the leader of the sect, who is no other than the master, Shoko Asahara," Hashimoto told the Tokyo District Court.
Dozens are on trial for murder and other charges related to the March 1995 sarin nerve gas attack on Tokyo's subway system in which 12 people died and thousands were made ill.

Police witnesses told the court on Thursday of the harrowing find of the almost unidentifiable bodies of Sakamoto, his wife Satoko and their one-year-old son Tatsuhiko, killed in 1989 allegedly on the orders of the cult head.
The remains were buried in three locations scattered across the mountains of central Japan. Before his disappearance, Sakamoto had organised a group of plaintiffs seeking redress from the cult.
Hashimoto choked back tears several times during his testimony as his former master, seated five yards (metres) away, repeatedly interrupted questioning with nonsensical outbursts.

Asahara, pale and amply filling out his dark blue tracksuit after more than 1-1/2 years in a detention centre, ranted incessantly as if conducting his own private trial with an imaginary cast of interlocutors.
Two cult members cross-examined on Friday, Tomomitsu Niimi and Tomomasa Nakagawa, refused to testify despite repeated questioning by prosecution and defence lawyers.
Niimi, a close confidant of the guru, told the court: "I refuse to testify on the grounds that doing so may affect the outcome of my own trial."
The trials of Niimi, Hashimoto and Nakagawa, charged along with Asahara with the Sakamoto murders, have yet to begin.
Asahara has failed to enter a plea on any of the 17 charges against him.
